title: John Korir, Sharon Lokedi win Boston Marathon for back-to-back men’s and women’s titles
content:
When reigning champion John Korir took the lead at the 20-mile mark in the Boston Marathon, he separated himself from the pack and continued to increase that distance for the next 6 miles. Korir crossed the finish line with outstretched hands and no competitors in sight as he won his second straight Boston Marathon men’s division title.

The Kenyan broke away from a five-man pack to pass Ethiopia’s Milkesa Mengesha at the mile marker and start his torrid final stretch. Korir held a 32-second lead by mile 23 and maintained his blistering speed to set a course record with an unofficial time of 2:01:52. He shaved nearly three minutes off his race-winning time of 2:04:45 last year.

Korir told NBC Boston that he “enjoyed” Monday’s race and “had no problems from the start to the finish.”

The 29-year-old set another mark with his 2025 Boston win by joining his brother, Wesley, the 2012 Boston Marathon winner, as the only set of brothers to win the elite marathon. John also won the Chicago Marathon in 2024.

Alphonce Felix Simbu finished second in the men’s field at 2:02:47, and Benson Kipruto closely followed at 2:02:50.

The women’s division also featured a familiar face, with Kenya’s Sharon Lokedi defending her Boston Marathon title in 2:18:51.

Lokedi finished nearly a minute before runner-up Loice Chemnung (2:19:35), and Mary Ngugi-Cooper ran a 2:20:07 to place third.

It was a tight women’s race with Lokedi and Americans Annie Frisbie and Jess McClain among the pack of eight runners at the 20-mile marker. Fellow Kenyans Irine Cheptai and Chemnung pulled ahead with Lokedi as they passed 21 miles, finally breaking up a crowded pack.

But Lokedi had gained more ground by mile 24 and held a 19-second lead over Chemnung to emerge as the expected winner.

Lokedi said she wasn’t sure how fast she was running once she took the lead and thought, “This is good rhythm. I’ll just stick with it for as long as I can,” per NBC Boston.

In the men’s wheelchair race, Marcel Hug of Switzerland won Monday, marking his ninth victory in Boston.

Hug finished with an unofficial time of 1:16:06, and trails Ernst van Dyk’s record of 10 titles. Hug fell 33 seconds shy of his course record of 1:15:33, set in 2024.

“Such a fantastic race,” Hug said. “I felt good from the beginning.”

The United States’ Daniel Romanchuk finished second in 1:22:44, while Jetze Plat of the Netherlands was third at 1:24:13.

In the women’s wheelchair race, Great Britain’s Eden Rainbow-Cooper won with a time of 1:30:51, marking her second win in Boston after taking the title in 2024.

Rainbow-Cooper called it “amazing” to win another marathon in Boston.

“The only way is up, so it means a lot to me,” she said.

Switzerland’s Catherine Debrunner came in second at 1:32:59, and American Tatyana McFadden finished third in 1:36:43.
